newsitem.title: CHINA: LME zinc seen testing $1,200, China not a factor.
newsitem.headline: LME zinc seen testing $1,200, China not a factor.

text.p: China's exit from world metals markets this week should not have much bearing on whether zinc breaches the important $1,200-a-tonne barrier in Monday trading on the London Metal Exchange, Far East traders said.
"I don't think the absence of the Chinese is going to significantly help it, going up or down," a Singapore-based trader said. "Zinc is range-bound, but sentiment is strong."

China, as well as many other Asian centres, has closed down to celebrate the arrival of the lunar new year. Most Chinese markets will be closed until February 17, though trading activity is expected to pick up towards the middle of this week.
The few Asian traders available on Monday said recent rallies in the LME zinc price were more an anticipation of coming tightness than a reflection of current fundamentals.
LME zinc hit a fresh two-year high of $1,196 a tonne in early Friday trading, ending the day $3 easier than its opening, at $1,183 a tonne.
What one Asian trader described as "the magical and psychological level" of $1,200 a tonne is the metal's next test, followed by the January 1995 peak of $1,239.

"We're still looking at a shortfall of at least 200,000 to 250,000 tonnes in (global) supply this year so there is definitely some justification for these price movements. Whether they are moving ahead of true tightness is the question," a producer representative said.

"But we see a trend upwards and we've been telling that to our customers for quite a while and we see an increase in forward buying to protect the contracts they've locked in for six months," he said.
Copper prices were seen by trading sources in Asia as attractive for producers in the near term.
LME copper ended the Friday kerb at the bottom of its range, hit by a bout of end-of-week profit-taking after prices failed to take the upside.
Three months copper finished the afternoon kerb at $2,239, down $18 a tonne from Thursday's close.
Tightness in availability of physical metal in some areas, including China, would help maintain short-term strength, another trader said.
"Anything from $2,100 forward seems to be attractive and even last week we saw some producer activity for the second half of 1997, going into 1998," he said.

"We would think that from here down it is probably a reasonable buying level. Although it has had a bit of a retracement overnight, the market looks to be relatively well supported and we'd much rather be on the long side than on the short side," he said.
